711.quote_or_event: “(If the pupil does not understand his short explanation), he should explain at greater length. When the pupil has heard it, he will correctly understand the Truth.”
711.explanation: The Sutrakritanga tells the preaching monk to fit his explanation to the hearer: briefly at first, then at greater length if the listener needs it, and never with long-winded explanations of difficult passages (1.14.23).
711.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes judging the audience a precondition of speaking well, so that words are weighed to suit those who hear them.
711.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.24 (cf. I.14.23) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
711._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on adjusting speech to the hearer; the Jain setting is a monk teaching doctrine, not a minister in a royal council.

712.quote_or_event: “To give way to: anger, pride, deceit and greed, laughter, fear, loquacity and slander; these eight faults should a well-disciplined monk avoid; he should use blameless and concise speech at the proper time.”
712.explanation: Bhāṣā-samiti, carefulness in speech, is one of the five samitis every Jain monk observes. It requires speech that is free of passion, sparing, and timed correctly.
712.tie_back: The Kural's call to choose the right moment and speak only after understanding fully matches the Jain rule of 'blameless and concise speech at the proper time'.
712.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 24.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
712._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on timing and purity of speech; the Jain rule is ascetic discipline rather than courtly eloquence.

713.quote_or_event: “He who correctly knows the sacred texts, who practises austerities, who understands all details of the Law, who is an authentic interpreter, clever, and learned--such a man is competent to explain the entire creed.”
713.explanation: The Sutrakritanga closes its lecture on the true monk by stating who is qualified to speak on the Law. By implication, one without that understanding should not take it up.
713.tie_back: The Kural says that whoever speaks without the needed understanding has no real ability; the Jain verse sets out the competence a speaker must have.
713.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
713._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable fit on competence as a precondition for speaking; the Jain text is about knowing the doctrine, not about knowing the assembly.

714.quote_or_event: “If he is not proud of his learning; if he does not find fault with others”
714.explanation: Among the fifteen qualities of the well-behaved monk, the Uttaradhyayana lists humility about one's learning; being 'proud of his learning' is among the faults of the ill-behaved (11.7).
714.tie_back: The Kural's advice to hide one's brilliance like plain white plaster before the dull is close to the Jain ideal of a learned person who does not show off.
714.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.10–13 (excerpt) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
714._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (an excerpt from the list in 11.10–13). Partial match: the Jain text praises humility about learning in general and has no counterpart to the Kural's tactic of shining among the learned and staying quiet among the dull.

715.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
715.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's discipline also tells the disciple 'He should not speak unasked' (1.14). Restraint of speech before the wise is part of vinaya, the humility that makes learning possible.
715.tie_back: This is the Kural's restraint of not rushing to speak first among wiser elders, stated almost word for word as a Jain rule of conduct.
715.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.8 (cf. 1.14) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
715._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one fit on not speaking forward in the presence of the wise; the Kural calls this the best of good things, which the Jain verse does not rank.

716.quote_or_event: “He should not pervert nor render obscure (the truth); he should fabricate neither text nor meaning, being a saviour; being devoted to the Teacher and considering well his words, he delivers faithfully what he has learned.”
716.explanation: The Jain expounder must speak with great care, because a slip in handing on the doctrine distorts the truth that others rely on.
716.tie_back: The Kural compares a slip of speech before the deeply learned to falling from the path, and the Jain verse likewise treats error in learned speech as a serious lapse to guard against.
716.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
716._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Next-best match: it stresses care and accuracy in speech, but not the Kural's particular danger of erring before an expert audience.

717.quote_or_event: “As water put into a shell shines with a doubled brilliancy, so do the piety, fame, and knowledge of a very learned monk.”
717.explanation: The lecture on 'The Very Learned' praises learning that shines all the more because of what holds it, opening a long series of similes for the learned monk.
717.tie_back: The Kural says learning shines brightest in the company of those who can judge words without flaw, and the Jain image likewise has learning gaining 'doubled brilliancy' from a fitting setting.
717.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
717._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the Jain simile is about the learned person as the vessel of knowledge, not about the audience as the setting where learning becomes visible.

718.quote_or_event: “(The teacher) takes delight in instructing a clever (pupil), just as the rider (in managing) a well-broken horse; but he tires to instruct a foolish (pupil), just as the rider (tires to manage) an unbroken horse.”
718.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that teaching depends on the receiver: instruction given to a capable hearer is a pleasure and bears fruit, while instruction given to a dull one wears out the teacher.
718.tie_back: This matches the Kural's point that speaking to those who already understand is like watering plants that are already growing.
718.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
718._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on speech bearing fruit in a receptive hearer; the Jain image is horsemanship, not watering a garden bed.

719.quote_or_event: “When reprimanded a wise man should not be angry, but he should be of a forbearing mood; he should not associate, laugh, and play with mean men.”
719.explanation: The Jain disciple is told to keep away from low company and not to take part in its idle talk and amusement.
719.tie_back: The Kural warns the good speaker never, even by forgetting himself, to hold forth before a mean assembly, and the Jain verse likewise keeps the disciplined person out of mean men's company.
719.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
719._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: it forbids mixing with mean men in general, not specifically speaking good things before them.

720.quote_or_event: “As a pig leaves a trough filled with grain to feed on faeces, so a brute (of a man) turns away from virtue, and takes to evil ways.”
720.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses this coarse image for the unfit pupil who turns from the good food of instruction to filth, and in the next verses says such a pupil is driven away.
720.tie_back: The Kural's nectar spilled into a gutter and the Jain pig leaving grain for filth both picture something precious wasted on those unfit to receive it.
720.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
720._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Next-best match: the imagery of good things versus filth is similar, but the Jain verse blames the unworthy receiver and gives no warning to the speaker about choosing an audience.
